justification: Forming a fresh judgement first, as a policy reviewer hunting low-value content: this article clears the bar comfortably and would not read as thin, templated or machine-produced to a reviewer. It is built around one escalating, falsifiable demonstration (Temperature -> Freezing -> HeatAdvisory -> a hand-applied mutation) rather than a 'what is code coverage' listicle, and it is honest about a real tool limitation instead of glossing over it: dotnet-stryker genuinely exits 1 against this pillar's file-based programs, shown with the actual log grep, not asserted as a claim. I re-fetched the current top comparators directly this round rather than trusting prior rounds' notes: Microsoft Learn's coverage tutorial is plain scaffolding-and-options reference prose with no worked branch-coverage-misses-a-bug demonstration; its mutation-testing page uses a synthetic PriceCalculator with console-report screenshots rather than captured, reproducible transcripts; Fowler's two bliki entries are quotable but non-executable; Codecov's 'line or branch coverage' post (re-fetched this round) is introductory Python-only material with no mutation testing, no boundary bugs, and no real execution traces at all, by its own content. This article's throughline -- the identical `<` vs `<=` mistake evading both line and branch coverage, then exposed as a surviving mutant -- is a genuinely original synthesis none of those pages attempt. Headings are specific to the content and do not echo sibling testing articles' structure or phrasing (checked against unit-testing-fundamentals, property-based-testing, test-doubles, testing-pyramid-and-integration-tests, test-driven-development, plus algorithms/binary-search and algorithms/recursion from another pillar -- all use distinct, sentence-like headings with no shared template, no boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion'); the four exercises vary in form (predict-the-percentage, find-the-bug-before-running, predict-which-mutant-survives, extend-the-code-and-verify) and none leaks its output above the collapsed solution. No filler intro/outro, no keyword stuffing, no formulaic triplets or 'it's not X, it's Y' tells, no invented experience or statistics, no dead-end navigation (both body links target already-published siblings, matching docs/crosslinks/testing/code-coverage.md, which correctly documents why no planned-but-unpublished link was needed). `node tools/check-article.mjs testing/code-coverage` passes clean (0 errors, 20 warnings, all cosmetic code-width, words=5634, prose=3052). I independently re-verified every quotation this article attributes to a source rather than trusting earlier rounds: Fowler's AssertionFreeTesting fragments ('made a big point of using heavy testing with JUnit', 'proudly showed the client all the tests and the green bar', 'there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests') are verbatim substrings of the live page; the Marick 'subtle difference' quote and the closing 'if a part of your test suite is weak...' quote are both correctly attributed to Brian Marick, matching the live page's own attribution; the dotnet-coverage 'such as console or Blazor' phrasing now matches the live page exactly; the Coverlet 'only supports modern .NET SDK-style projects' quote is verbatim from the live README; and Microsoft's mutant definition, the equivalent-operator table row ('x < y becomes x <= y'), and the 'don't chase a 100% mutation score' note are all verbatim from the live mutation-testing page. A targeted web search for five distinctive sentences of the article's own prose (not sourced quotes) found no matching or near-matching text anywhere online, so there is no copying or close paraphrase to flag. This round's specific job is to check round 2's findings were fixed at the root, not papered over, so I re-verified each independently: the technical critic's round-2 blocker -- the 'Predict which mutant survives' exercise wrongly claiming a 32->33 threshold shift is 'killed' when it actually survives against the article's own three tests -- is fixed correctly, not fudged: the current solution states 'Mutation 1 survives', gives the correct reasoning (none of the three tests, at 20/32/50, falls in the (32, 33] gap the shift opens), and I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/code-coverage.md` five separate times this round (isolated, no other process touching this worktree): five clean passes (blocks=40, executed=20 every time), confirming the corrected mutation-threshold block's output is genuinely reproducible, not a one-off. The technical critic's round-2 minor -- Coverlet named for its vocabulary but silently dropped for dotnet-coverage with no explanation -- is also fixed: the article now explains, correctly and citing Coverlet's own README, that every Coverlet driver (VSTest collector, MSBuild task, Microsoft Testing Platform integration) assumes a project file the same way Stryker.NET does, which is why a file-based program needs dotnet-coverage's process-level attach instead. Neither fix is cosmetic wording around the same defect: the mutation exercise's answer key is now factually correct and independently reproducible, and the Coverlet gap is genuinely explained rather than left for the reader to infer. Nothing here clears my bar for a 10 (reserved for a page indistinguishable from or better than the best possible treatment with no notes at all whatsoever), but this is comfortably above the 8.5 ships-with-nits-only anchor: a reader who put this next to Microsoft Learn's or Codecov's coverage of the same territory would come away with a sharper, more falsifiable understanding of exactly what a coverage percentage can and cannot tell them, and every issue that held it back across two prior rounds is resolved at the root.
